items.title: Section: Precisely Defining "Wrongly Grasped Emptiness" — Emptiness Is Always Relational

items.zh: 謂有沙門、或婆羅門，由彼故空亦不信受，於此而空亦不信受，如是名為惡取空者。
items.en: There are certain ascetics or brahmins who neither accept that a given thing is empty of what genuinely is not present in it, nor accept that, by virtue of this, what remains genuinely is present — such a person is called one who wrongly grasps emptiness.

items.zh: 何以故？由彼故空，彼實是無；於此而空，此實是有。由此道理可說為空。若說一切都無所有，何處、何者、何故名空？亦不應言由此、於此即說為空。是故名為惡取空者。
items.en: Why is this? Because a thing is empty of what is genuinely absent from it, and by virtue of this, what remains is genuinely present — it is only for this reason that "emptiness" can be spoken of at all. But if one says that everything whatsoever is nonexistent, then where, of what, and for what reason could "emptiness" even be named? Nor should one say that mere nonexistence itself, taken by itself, is what "emptiness" means. For this reason, such a person is called one who wrongly grasps emptiness.

items.title: Section: "Correctly Grasping Emptiness" — Neither Superimposing, Nor Denying, Nor Grasping, Nor Abandoning

items.zh: 謂由於此彼無所有，即由彼故正觀為空；復由於此餘實是有，即由餘故如實知有。如是名為悟入空性，如實無倒。
items.en: Because a given thing is genuinely without what it is imputed to have, one correctly regards it, on that very basis, as empty; and because what remains beyond that is genuinely present, one truly knows, on that very basis, that it exists. This is called genuinely entering into the nature of emptiness, truly and without distortion.

items.zh: 謂於如前所說一切色等想事、所說色等假說性法，都無所有，是故於此色等想事，由彼色等假說性法說之為空。於此一切色等想事，何者為餘？謂即色等假說所依。如是二種皆如實知。謂於此中實有唯事，於唯事中亦有唯假；
不於實無起增益執，不於實有起損減執。不增不減、不取不捨，如實了知如實真如離言自性。如是名為善取空者，於空法性能以正慧妙善通達。
items.en: One does not generate a superimposing attachment towards what is genuinely absent, nor a denying attachment towards what genuinely exists. Neither adding nor subtracting, neither grasping nor abandoning, one truly understands, exactly as it is, suchness and the inexpressible nature. This is called one who correctly grasps emptiness, able to penetrate the true nature of emptiness with genuine, excellent wisdom.

items.title: Reasoning Closes; Scriptural Testimony Opens with "Within This, That Is Not Found"

items.zh: 如是隨順證成道理，應知諸法離言自性。復由至教，應知諸法離言自性。
items.en: In accordance with this reasoning of valid demonstration, it should be understood that phenomena possess an inexpressible nature. Furthermore, by scriptural authority as well, it should be understood that phenomena possess an inexpressible nature.

items.zh: 如佛世尊轉有經中，為顯此義而說頌曰：以彼彼諸名，詮彼彼諸法；此中無有彼，是諸法法性。
items.en: As the World-Honoured Buddha, in the Ativṛtta-sūtra, said in verse to reveal this very meaning: "By this or that name, this or that phenomenon is described; within this, that is not found — this is the true nature of phenomena."

items.zh: 云何此頌顯如是義？謂於色等想法，建立色等法名；即以如是色等法名，詮表隨說色等想法。或說為色，或說為受，或說為想，廣說乃至說為涅槃。於此一切色等想法、色等自性都無所有，亦無有餘色等性法，而於其中色等想法離言義性，真實是有。當知即是勝義自性，亦是法性。

items.title: Section: The Second Citation — "One Water, Four Perceptions": Seeing and Hearing Without Craving

items.zh: 又佛世尊義品中說：世間諸世俗，牟尼皆不著，無著、孰能取，見、聞而不愛。
items.en: Moreover, the World-Honoured Buddha said in the Arthavarga: "Every worldly convention — the sage is unattached to all of it. Being unattached, who then could grasp anything? He sees and hears, yet without craving."

items.zh: 云何此頌顯如是義？謂於世間色等想事，所有色等種種假說，名諸世俗。
如彼假說於此想事有其自性，如是世俗牟尼不著。何以故？以無增益、損減見故，無有現前顛倒見故，由此道理名為不著。如是無著，誰復能取？由無見故，於事不取增益、損減，於所知境能正觀察，故名為見；聽聞所知境界言說，故名為聞。依此見聞，貪愛不生，亦不增長，唯於彼緣畢竟斷滅，安住上捨，故名不愛。
items.en: Whatever self-nature such imputation asserts of a given event conceived through perception, the sage remains unattached to this worldly convention regarding it ... because of holding no distorted view, he neither superimposes nor denies with respect to any event, and is able to correctly observe the object of knowledge — this is called "seeing" ... on the basis of this seeing and hearing, craving does not arise and does not increase; with respect to that object it is utterly extinguished, and he abides in supreme equanimity — this is called "without craving."

items.title: Section: The Third Citation — Meditating on Nothing at All, Praised by Gods Who Cannot Even Perceive It

items.zh: 又佛世尊為彼散他迦多衍那作如是說：散他苾芻！不依於地而修靜慮，不依於水、不依於火、不依於風、不依空處、不依識處、不依無所有處、不依非想非非想處、不依此世他世、不依日月光輪、不依見聞覺知、不依所求所得、不依意隨尋伺、不依一切而修靜慮。
items.en: Moreover, the World-Honoured Buddha spoke thus to the monk Sandha Kātyāyana: "Monk Sandha! Do not cultivate concentration resting on earth, nor resting on water, fire, or wind; nor resting on the sphere of space, the sphere of consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception; nor resting on this world or another world; nor resting on the light of sun or moon; nor resting on what is seen, heard, sensed, or known; nor resting on what is sought or attained; nor resting on the mind's own deliberation and reflection — cultivate concentration resting on nothing whatsoever."

items.zh: 云何修習靜慮苾芻，不依於地而修靜慮，廣說乃至不依一切而修靜慮？[＊]
散他苾芻！或有於地除遣地想，或有於水除遣水想，廣說乃至或於一切除一切想，如是修習靜慮苾芻，不依於地而修靜慮，廣說乃至不依一切而修靜慮。如是修習靜慮苾芻，為因陀羅、為伊舍那、為諸世主并諸天眾遙為作禮而讚頌曰：敬禮吉祥士，敬禮士中尊，我今不知汝，依何修靜慮。
items.en: "Monk Sandha! With respect to earth, one eliminates the percept of earth; with respect to water, one eliminates the percept of water — and so on in detail, up to eliminating, with respect to all things, the percept of all things." ... A monk who cultivates concentration in this way is bowed to from afar by Indra, by Īśāna, by all the lords of the world, and by the assembled gods, who praise him in verse: "Homage to this excellent being, homage to the most honoured among beings — we do not know what you rely on to cultivate concentration."

blocks.text: The famous definition of "correctly grasping emptiness", followed by three scriptural passages that support the argument. This short definition is one of the most quoted passages in Yogācāra literature.

"Some ascetics neither accept that a thing is empty of what is genuinely not present in it, nor accept that what remains is genuinely present." "A thing is empty of what is absent from it, and what remains is present: only for this reason can 'emptiness' be spoken of at all. But if everything is nonexistent, then where, of what, and by what could anything be empty?"

"Because a thing is genuinely without what it is imputed to have, one regards it as empty; and because what remains is genuinely present, one knows it exists." "Neither adding nor subtracting, neither grasping nor abandoning, one understands suchness and the inexpressible nature exactly as it is."

items: A verse: "By this or that name, this or that phenomenon is described; within this, that is not found: this is the true nature of phenomena."
From the *Arthavarga*: "Every worldly convention, the sage is unattached to all of it. Being unattached, who could grasp anything? He sees and hears, yet without craving."

To the monk Sandha Kātyāyana: "Do not cultivate concentration resting on earth, water, fire, wind, nor on the formless spheres, nor on this world or the next." One who meditates thus "is bowed to from afar by Indra and the gods, who cannot perceive on what he meditates".

blocks.text: The definition is subtle: emptiness is always emptiness *of* something, and what it is empty of is the imagined nature; what remains is real. This is the Yogācāra reading of emptiness, against both naive realism and nihilism.

quiz.q: "Certain ascetics or brahmins … wrongly grasp emptiness." What four kinds of ascetic does Master Cháng Bǎi list?
quiz.why: "There are certain ascetics or brahmins who neither accept … — such a person is called one who wrongly grasps emptiness." Master Cháng Bǎi: there are four kinds of renunciant ascetic — those who conquer by the path, teach the path, live by the path, and corrupt the path.

quiz.q: "Empty of that, which is genuinely absent." What everyday example does Master Cháng Bǎi give?
quiz.why: "Why is this? Because a thing is empty of what is genuinely absent from it, and by virtue of this, what remains is genuinely present." Master Cháng Bǎi: for example, when you say "dumpling," no dumpling is present — that's "empty of that, which is genuinely absent."

quiz.q: One who correctly grasps emptiness "penetrates with genuine wisdom." How does this differ from wrongly grasping, per the masters?
options: Miào Jìng: grasping with ignorance is wrong, with wisdom right; Cháng Bǎi: wrong grasping holds a sign — clinging to a real emptiness
quiz.why: "This is called one who correctly grasps emptiness, able to penetrate the true nature of emptiness with genuine, excellent wisdom." Venerable Miào Jìng: grasping with ignorance is wrongly grasping emptiness; grasping with wisdom is correctly grasping it. Master Cháng Bǎi: wrongly grasped emptiness is sign-holding grasping — clinging to the mark of emptiness, to a real emptiness.

quiz.q: "As the Buddha said in verse in the 轉有經." How does Venerable Miào Jìng explain the title?
options: 轉 means extinguishing; 有 the three existences — desire, form, formless
quiz.why: "As the World-Honoured Buddha, in the Ativṛtta-sūtra, said in verse to reveal this very meaning: 'By this or that name, this or that phenomenon is described; within this, that is not found — this is the true nature of phenomena.'" Venerable Miào Jìng: 轉 means extinguishing; 有 is the three existences — desire, form, and formless.

quiz.q: "The Buddha said in the 義品" — rendered confidently as "Arthavarga." What do the lectures say?
options: Cháng Bǎi lists three views (Jǐng, Kuījī, Wŏnch'ŭk); Miào Jìng only says the canon has such a text
quiz.why: "Moreover, the World-Honoured Buddha said in the Arthavarga: 'Every worldly convention — the sage is unattached to all of it.'" Master Cháng Bǎi: Kuījī says it's the 義品 in the Abhidharma; Wŏnch'ŭk says it's part of the 轉有經 (Jǐng gives a third view). Venerable Miào Jìng: the canon contains a text called 義品. The English settles on "Arthavarga"; the lectures don't.

quiz.q: "Bowed to by Indra, by Īśāna, by the lords of the world." How do the lectures identify them?
options: Cháng Bǎi: Indra is Śakra, Īśāna the Paranirmita-vaśavartin god, the world-lord Mahābrahmā; Miào Jìng: the world-lord is the first-dhyāna Brahmā king
quiz.why: "A monk who cultivates concentration in this way is bowed to from afar by Indra, by Īśāna, by all the lords of the world, and by the assembled gods." Master Cháng Bǎi: Indra is Śakra, Īśāna is the god of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, the world-lord is Mahābrahmā. Venerable Miào Jìng: it's Brahmā, the Brahmā king of the first dhyāna.
